procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 22nd January 1953 of the Election Tribunal, Yellore in Election Petition No. 35 of 1952.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There is no mention of High Court proceedings in the provided text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order of the Election Tribunal. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in limine (at the threshold).

issue.issue_text: whether the appellant was disqualified under s. 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for election to the House of the People.

facts: The appellant was elected to the House of the People.
An election petition was filed against him on the grounds that he was disqualified under Section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
The basis for the disqualification claim was that the appellant had an existing contract with the Government of India's Postal Department to transport postal articles and mail bags.
The appellant admitted to having this contract.
law: The case centered on the interpretation of Section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
This section disqualifies a person from being a member of Parliament if they have a contract for the "performance of any service undertaken by the appropriate Government."
application: The appellant argued that his contract did not fall under the disqualification clause.
His contention was that carrying mail is an "exclusive privilege" and a "normal function" of the government, not a "service undertaken by the Government" within the meaning of the Act.
The Election Tribunal rejected the appellant's argument and held that he was disqualified.
The appellant then appealed this decision to the Supreme Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appeal, thereby overturning the Election Tribunal's decision and ruling that the appellant was not disqualified. The provided text details the appellant's argument that his contract was for a 'normal function' of government rather than a disqualifying 'service,' but the text itself does not contain the Supreme Court's specific reasoning for why it accepted this position and reached its final conclusion.

issue.issue_text: Has this Tribunal no jurisdiction td decide the question as regards the disqualification of the returned candidate, because of article 103 of the Constitution of India?

facts: An election petition was filed challenging the appellant's election to the House of the People.
In his defense before the Election Tribunal, the appellant contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide on his disqualification.
law: The appellant's argument was based on Article 103 of the Constitution of India, which states that the question of a member's disqualification is to be decided by the President, whose decision shall be final.
application: The Election Tribunal considered the appellant's argument regarding its jurisdiction.
The Tribunal held that Article 103 of the Constitution was not a bar to its jurisdiction and proceeded to decide the case.

When the case was appealed to the Supreme Court, the appellant did not raise the objection to the Tribunal's jurisdiction again. The text states, 'In this appeal the contentions raised before the Election Tribunal, except the objection to the Tribunal's jurisdiction in view of the provisions of article...'
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide this specific issue because the appellant did not raise it on appeal. The issue was decided by the Election Tribunal, which rejected the appellant's contention and affirmed its own jurisdiction to hear the matter. This part of the Tribunal's decision was not challenged before the Supreme Court.

arguments.issue_text: whether the appellant was disqualified under s. 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for election to the House of the People.
appellant_arguments: The Central Government had not 'undertaken' any 'service' within the meaning of section 7(d) of the Act when it made arrangements for the carriage of mail bags and postal articles through the appellant.
The appellant had no hand in the fixing of the remuneration to be paid by the Postal Department for carrying its mails.
respondent_arguments: The government, in its Postal Department, has undertaken a service to be rendered to the community, and such a service is a 'service' within the meaning of section 7(d) of the Act.
The agreement between the appellant and the Central Government for carrying mail was a contract for the performance of a service undertaken by the government, which results in disqualification.

arguments.issue_text: Has this Tribunal no jurisdiction td decide the question as regards the disqualification of the returned candidate, because of article 103 of the Constitution of India?
appellant_arguments: The Election Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to decide the issue of disqualification in view of the provisions of Article 103 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The Election Tribunal has the proper jurisdiction to decide on the disqualification of the candidate.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An agreement between two competent parties with their free consent and for a lawful cash consideration is a valid contract, even if made in pursuance of a statutory rule, when the party enters into it with full knowledge of their rights and liabilities under it.
obiter: A party could have been circumspect enough to insert an alternative clause into a surety bond to give a court's judgment or order the same effect as contemplated by the terms of the bond.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that the appellant's contract to transport mail bags and postal articles for the Central Government disqualified him under section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The court reasoned that even if providing postal services is not an obligatory sovereign duty, it is a "service undertaken" by the government for the convenience of the public. Therefore, having an interest in a contract for the performance of such a service falls squarely within the scope of the disqualification intended by the Act.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation of "service undertaken by the appropriate Government" under s. 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which does not require the service to be an obligatory sovereign function but merely one that the government has chosen to provide to the community.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's argument that the Central Government had not 'undertaken' a 'service' by arranging for mail carriage, finding that the government's provision of postal facilities for public convenience qualifies as such a service.

The court found no substance in the appellant's contentions, noting that he entered into the contract voluntarily with his eyes open, knowing his rights and liabilities, and that no one is compelled to enter into such a contract for transporting postal articles.
The argument that the appellant had no hand in fixing the remuneration was implicitly dismissed as irrelevant to the existence of a disqualifying contract.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed with the respondent's position that the government, in its Postal Department, has undertaken a service to be rendered to the community, and this is a 'service' within the meaning of section 7(d) of the Act.

The court determined that the appellant's agreement was a straightforward illustration of the kind of contract for the performance of a service undertaken by the government that is contemplated by s. 7(d) of the Act.
policy_considerations: Section 7 of the Act is clearly intended to avoid a conflict between public duty and private interests.
